newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African arms sale could tilt Mideast balance.
newsitem.headline: S.African arms sale could tilt Mideast balance.

text.p: A battle-tank upgrade that South Africa wants to sell to Syria would put Syrian tanks on a par with Israel's after decades of being outgunned, military experts say.
The proposed sale could tilt the military balance dangerously in the Middle East, or stabilise it by deterring an attack by better-armed Israeli forces.
It depends on your point of view.

Providing Syria with a state-of-the-art targeting system for its ageing Soviet-built T-72 tanks would incur the wrath of the United States, which views Damascus as a sponsor of international terrorism.

The "Tiger New-generation Fire Control System", as it is called, is a computer-based range-finding and aiming system which uses lasers, advanced optics and thermal imaging to improve ability to fire on the move and at night.

According to news reports in South Africa, the system -- which is used in the country's Olifant main battle tank, Rooikat armoured car and G6 self-propelled gun -- would lift the T-72's first-shot hit rates from 60 percent to over 90 percent.

That, say experts, would put Syrian gunners on a par with Israel's Merkava tank, which has outgunned them for more than 20 years. It would extend the life of the T-72 by 10 to 15 years, according to some reports.
Exports also say the Tiger system was developed by South Africa using U.S. and Israeli technology.

Technology leakage could only heighten U.S. hostility to a proposed arms contract with a state which Washington says promotes terrorism, and one that its ally Israel sees as a main foe still not committed to a Middle East peace pact.

Under U.S. law, doing an arms deal with Damascus would lead automatically to a cut-off of certain forms of aid which South Africa receives. However, the value of that disappearing aid would be a lot less than the reported $650 million that the tank deal would earn.

Spitting in the eye of the superpower is hardly calculated to be good for trade and investment, which are South African priorities, but the government of President Nelson Mandela was incensed when Washington publicly warned it off the deal.

Mandela and his ruling party fought a bitter struggle for their freedom from white supremacy when many countries, including the United States, were still willing to do business with the apartheid regime. They don't like being pushed around, as they would see it.

Mandela also wants to demonstrate by actions as well as words that the old South African alliance with Israel against the Arab states no longer holds, and that his government is determined to pursue what it sees as a more balanced policy.

South African arms exports are supposed to be governed by the National Conventional Arms Control Committee (NCACC), established about 16 months ago on guidelines similar to U.N. principles for the sale of lethal weapons.
Sales should not harm human rights, help terrorism, escalate conflict, or harm the exporting state's own trade and diplomatic interests, the NCACC guidelines say.
Whether or not any or all of these principles would be violated by a sale to Syria is for the South African government to decide.

Last May, NCACC chairman Kader Asmal said arms trade with Syria, Turkey, Sri Lanka, Iran and North and Soyth Korea was under review whereas Nigeria, Libya, Sudan, Liberia, Afghanistan and Iraq were listed as no-go areas.
Whatever the government decides in the end on the Syria deal is very unlikely to convince the party it offends by its choice.

The Arab market is a potential goldmine for South Africa's sales-hungry arms industry, and Syria could unlock it. But the cost of offending the United States must give the Mandela government great pause for thought.
